notes: \cpara{Describes semantic priming in a word-recognition task. Wikipedia's article ``Priming (psychology)'' says that ``semantic, associative, and form priming are well established,'' while ``some longer-term priming effects were not replicated.'' The priming findings that failed to replicate were of another kind (see the notes on the last paragraph).}
\cpara{Points out that priming acts on word recognition, a step one would expect to come before thinking about meaning.}
\cpara{Takes priming as a sign that activation spreads to many associated words at once; the other words are offered with ``probably.''}

\cpara{Stated as fact, with no source. ``Unstoppable'' was disputed before the post. Stolz and Besner (\textsc{Current Directions in Psychological Science}, 1999) argued against the view that reading activates meaning automatically, concluding that ``Semantic processing depends strongly on attentional control over how activation is distributed across different levels of representation.''}
\cpara{Suggests the Stroop test as a home demonstration: the word's meaning gets in the way of naming its color.}

\cpara{Reports the experiment correctly. It is Study 1 of Mussweiler and Strack (\textsc{Journal of Personality and Social Psychology}, 2000), with 28 students and German words such as ``kalt'' (cold) and ``Sonne'' (sun). I could not check the 1999 review the post cites.}
\cpara{Names the general finding, that irrelevant or known-false information affects estimates and decisions: ``contamination.''}

\cpara{Restates the wheel study and the adjustment account. The detail of stopping ``at one end of a confidence interval'' is not in the 1974 paper cited for it, which says only that ``adjustments are typically insufficient.''}

\cpara{Revises the account of ``Anchoring and Adjustment,'' posted a month earlier (see the note there), without saying that it does. That post called adjustment ``The current theory'' for the wheel experiment; this one attributes most anchoring to contamination.}

\cfact{Offered with ``seems,'' and in line with the cited paper. Epley and Gilovich (2001) report that ``a consensus that none takes place seems to be emerging'' about adjustment, and argue that adjustment does occur when people produce the anchor themselves.}
\cpara{Rests ``shown to work'' on one paper, Wansink, Kent and Hoch (1998).}

\cpara{Links contamination to confirmation bias. The link has a basis in the post's sources. In the selective accessibility account the post cites, answering an anchor question means testing whether the anchor is right, and people ``evaluate hypotheses by attempting to confirm them'' (Epley and Gilovich's summary, 2001).}

\clogic{Unsupported by the post's evidence. Its studies measure how fast words are recognized and what estimates people give in the same session. None measures whether a primed idea lasts, so nothing shown here ``ensures'' an idea's continued existence.}

\cpara{The last step goes from recognizing words to holding conclusions, with no evidence in between. ``A single fleeting image can be enough to prime associated words for recognition'' is about word recognition. ``The bottom line is already decided'' is about beliefs. The post shows the first and asserts the second.}

\cfact{After the post, several findings that brief primes change later judgments and behavior failed to replicate. Doyen and colleagues (\textsc{PLoS ONE}, 2012) could not reproduce slower walking after primes about old age. In the Many Labs project (2014), ``flag priming influencing conservatism and currency priming influencing system justification'' ``did not replicate.'' The post could not have known of these failures. The word-recognition priming it opens with has held up.}
